title: Lily Rabe and Marsha Stephanie Blake can scream at me all night long ...
transcript: How do you handle a Shakespeare play with a really jarring tonal shift halfway through, complete with a new setting and new characters? Well, after seeing six productions of it, I feel like I finally get it. New York’s Shakespeare in the park is currently doing The Winter's Tale, a fascinating but notoriously tricky play. But even though this production seems on the surface kind of traditionalist, kind of unimaginative, I think the director, Daniel Sullivan, is quietly making choices that give the play more coherence and clarity than it usually has, in my experience. Famously, we go from this heavy drama in a royal palace about a king who deludes himself into believing his wife is cheating on him to basically a romantic comedy in a pastoral countryside for Act 4, which I believe is the longest act in all of Shakespeare. But I think this production, especially with the live loot player and everything, has this tender, melancholic feel that runs through the whole thing. This play is often described not as a comedy or tragedy, but as one of Shakespeare's “Romance” plays. And it is that sort of “Romantic” quality that brings everything together. The tragic, jealous romance and the forbidden lovers in the pastoral Act 4 feeling like two sides of the same coin. One of the other things that makes this play tricky is that in those first three acts, focusing on Leontes and Hermione, it doesn't feel like there's that much progression because he kind of arrives at this conclusion very early and doesn't deviate from it. But on this viewing, it felt like we're not so much tracking his character progression as much as the effects of his actions slowly spreading like a cancer to everyone around him. And while a lot of people are complaining this production is too long at about 3 hours and 20 minutes, I think letting us feel the passage of time kind of amplifies that effect. I have to say though, unfortunately, I am a big fan of Raul Esparza normally, but I think this performance was a big misfire. I think he was doing way too much. It rang very false to me. It was, like, hyper affected to the point of being almost unintentionally comedic. Or if the comedy was intentional, it was very out of step with everyone else around him. Still, though, otherwise, I do think this production makes a solid case for a play that I've often found very challenging. As a little disclaimer, I guess I don't know how much of that was this production, which was otherwise not all that extraordinary, versus how much was just the fact that I've now seen it six times.
classificationReason: Creator explicitly names Shakespeare in the Park's current production of The Winter's Tale, names director Daniel Sullivan, and stars Lily Rabe and Marsha Stephanie Blake. Offers substantive first-hand critical opinion about the production's tonal coherence, staging choices, and the live lute player.
